snpscaper lets you explore how human genetic variation is distributed
within and between populations around the world, using real genome data
from the 1000 Genomes Project. You choose a gene or a region of the genome;
snpscaper fetches the data and helps you analyse and plot it, all inside R.

This vignette introduces the key ideas and the basic workflow. Other
vignettes cover [population structure](population-structure.html) (PCA,
admixture and Fst), [diversity and selection](diversity-and-selection.html)
(heterozygosity, allele frequencies and linkage disequilibrium), and
[making reports](reports.html).

## Key ideas

### Genomes, SNPs and genotypes

The human genome is about 3 billion DNA letters long, spread over 22 pairs
of autosomes plus the sex chromosomes. Any two people's genomes are about
99.9% identical. Most of the differences are **SNPs** (single nucleotide
polymorphisms): positions where some people carry one letter, say `G`, and
others carry another, say `A`. The two versions are called **alleles**.

Because we inherit one copy of each autosome from each parent, everyone
carries two alleles at every SNP. At a SNP with alleles `G` and `A`, a
person can be `GG`, `GA` or `AA`. snpscaper records this **genotype** as
the number of copies of one of the alleles (the "alternative" allele, here
`A`): 0, 1 or 2.

### Reference and alternative alleles

Every SNP has a **reference** allele, the letter found in the human
reference genome, and an **alternative** allele. The reference genome was
assembled mostly from a few individuals, so the reference allele is simply
a convention: it is not necessarily the ancestral allele, nor the more
common one. Always check which allele a frequency refers to.

### Genome positions and GRCh38

Positions in the genome are given as a chromosome and a number of DNA
letters from its start, for example `chr2:135,851,076`. These coordinates
depend on the version of the reference genome. snpscaper uses the current
version, **GRCh38** (also called hg38), as do Ensembl and the UCSC Genome
Browser by default.

### The 1000 Genomes Project

The [1000 Genomes Project](https://www.internationalgenome.org) sequenced
the genomes of people from 26 populations, grouped into five continental
**super-populations**. snpscaper uses the 2,504 unrelated people from the
project, whose genomes were later re-sequenced at high coverage by the New
York Genome Center.

```{r}
library(snpscaper)

table(samples_1kg$super_pop)
head(samples_1kg)
```

| Code | Super-population | Populations |
|---|---|---|
| AFR | African | ACB, ASW, ESN, GWD, LWK, MSL, YRI |
| AMR | Admixed American | CLM, MXL, PEL, PUR |
| EAS | East Asian | CDX, CHB, CHS, JPT, KHV |
| EUR | European | CEU, FIN, GBR, IBS, TSI |
| SAS | South Asian | BEB, GIH, ITU, PJL, STU |

A few things are worth knowing about these populations. "Admixed American"
populations have recent ancestry from several continents (Indigenous
American, European and African). ASW (African Ancestry in Southwest US)
and ACB (African Caribbean in Barbados) also have mixed recent ancestry.
Some populations were sampled away from their region of origin, for example
CEU (Utah residents with Northern and Western European ancestry) and GIH
(Gujarati Indians in Houston).

### VCF files

Genotype data are usually stored in **VCF** (variant call format) files:
large text files with one line per variant and one column per person. The
1000 Genomes Project publishes one compressed VCF file per chromosome,
each tens of gigabytes. snpscaper never downloads a whole file. Each file
has a small **index** that records where each part of the chromosome is
stored, so snpscaper reads only the part you ask for.

## The basic workflow

### 1. Fetch a region

`fetch_region()` takes gene symbols or coordinates:

```{r eval = FALSE}
lct <- fetch_region("LCT")
mc1r <- fetch_region("MC1R", flank = 10000) # 10 kb either side of the gene
neutral <- fetch_region("chr18:1,000,000-1,300,000")
```

For genes, a flanking region (25 kb by default) is added on each side,
because variants that control a gene's activity often lie just outside it.
The main lactase persistence variant, for example, sits 14 kb upstream of
the LCT gene.

The first fetch needs an internet connection and takes from a few seconds
to a minute. The data are then saved on your computer, so fetching the same
region again is instant and works offline (see `?clear_cache`).

This vignette uses `example_lct`, a copy of `fetch_region("LCT")` that comes
with the package:

```{r}
lct <- example_lct
lct
```

The result is a `snpscape` object. It holds the genotypes (a table with one
row per person and one column per SNP), a description of each SNP, a
description of each person, and a record of where the data came from and
what has been done to them.

```{r}
lct$genotypes[1:5, 1:4]
head(lct$variants)
```

### 2. Choose genes to explore

The package includes a set of genes that make good teaching examples, with a
short description of each and one or two key SNPs:

```{r}
teaching_genes[, c("gene", "chrom", "description")]
teaching_snps[, c("gene", "rsid", "note")]
```

Any other gene can be fetched by its official symbol. Use `find_gene()` to
check where it is, and `find_snp()` to look up an rs number.

### 3. Filter SNPs

Most SNPs in the genome are very rare, and most analyses work better on a
cleaned-up set. `filter_snps()` removes rare SNPs and SNPs with many missing
genotypes, and can also remove SNPs that are strongly correlated with their
neighbours (LD pruning; see `?filter_snps` for why this matters).

```{r}
lct_common <- filter_snps(lct, min_maf = 0.01)
lct_pruned <- filter_snps(lct, min_maf = 0.01, prune_ld = TRUE)
lct_pruned
```

Of the 1,922 SNPs in the LCT region, only about one in five has a minor
allele frequency of 1% or more, and LD pruning keeps only a small fraction
of those. The LCT region has unusually strong LD because of recent
selection, as the [diversity and selection](diversity-and-selection.html)
vignette explains.

### 4. Choose populations

`keep_pops()` narrows the data to the populations you want to compare:

```{r}
lct_subset <- keep_pops(lct_common, pop = c("YRI", "GBR", "FIN", "CHB", "PJL"))
summary(lct_subset)
```

`summary()` lists the people per population and every processing step.

### 5. Analyse and plot

From here, every analysis follows the same pattern: a `calc_*()` function
calculates the numbers as a table, and a `plot_*()` function draws them. For
example, the frequency of the lactase persistence allele in each
population:

```{r}
freqs <- calc_allele_freqs(lct)
freqs[freqs$rsid %in% "rs4988235", c("pop", "super_pop", "ref", "alt", "alt_freq")]
```

```{r fig.height = 4}
plot_freqs(freqs, snp = "rs4988235")
```

The persistence allele (`A` on the genome's forward strand; it is usually
described as `T`, because LCT is read from the opposite strand) is common in
Northern Europe, present at lower frequencies in South Asia and in admixed
populations, and absent from the East Asian samples.

All plots are ordinary ggplot2 objects, so you can change them in the usual
way, for example by adding `+ ggplot2::labs(title = "My title")`.
